settings.title: Be the answer: how an engine decides who to name
settings.caption: Be the answer. Narrated, with captions. Written by Thomas D'Souza, Founder.
settings.fallback: Your browser does not play video. The five chapters beside it tell the same story.
settings.description: A narrated animated film: a customer asks an engine who to call, the engine asks three things (can I read it, do others confirm it, do people choose it), and raising all three changes the answer.
settings.transcript: This is Sam. He's the best plumber in town. But his phone is quiet. When a customer has a leak, she doesn't call Sam. She asks Google, Maps or ChatGPT: who should I call? Every engine decides the same way. It asks three things. Can I read what this business does? Do other sources confirm it? Do real people choose it? The three multiply. If one is zero, the answer is zero. So the engine names someone else. We fix all three. Read: Sam's site now says plainly what he does, where, and for whom. Confirm: listings, reviews and mentions that say the same thing. Choose: a listing people pick, and calls that prove it. Same question. Now every engine has a reason to name Sam. That is the D'Souza Equation. Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose. Be the answer.

settings.title: How does a search engine optimization company in the USA make you the answer?

settings.editor: With one equation that every engine obeys. Google, Maps, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity look different, but each does one job: take a person's question and name the most relevant business it can trust.
They differ in how they read. They agree on what they are looking for.

“Engines change. Your customer's question does not. Work on the question and every engine finds you.”

Thomas D'Souza, Founder, Relevant Search Media. In writing since 2025.

items.q: How many SEO agencies are there in the USA?

items.q: What is a search engine optimization company in the USA supposed to do?
items.a: Make your business the answer to the searches your customers make. In 2026 that means Google, Google Maps and the AI engines together. We map every search for your trade and city, run 413 checks, fix the biggest things first, and log each item with its link, so you can see the work every day.

items.q: Is there an affordable SEO company in the USA that still does real work?
items.a:
Affordable means the work is worth what it costs, and you can see it. Every plan is month to month, with no setup fee and no add-ons to buy.

Live work goes up by day 5, each item is logged with its link, and a report arrives every 15 days. Prices are discussed on the discovery call.

items.q: How soon will I see results?
items.a: Live work goes up on day 5 and your first report arrives on day 15. Rankings usually start moving between day 30 and day 60. By the end of month 4, at least half the customer searches in your map reach page one of Google, or we keep working at no charge until they do.

items.q: Can you get my business recommended by ChatGPT?
items.a: We do the work the AI engines use to choose a business: facts they can read, independent sources that confirm them, and signs that real people choose you. items.q: Will you also work with my competitors?
items.a:
No. We take one business per trade per city.

Two roofers in the same city cannot both be the business an engine names, so your slot is yours for as long as you stay. The Open Board shows which trades and cities are taken.

items.q: Can I cancel, and what do I keep?
items.a:
Every plan is month to month. You cancel by email.

You keep everything: the website, the content, the listings and every account, from day one. Nothing is held back and nothing is charged to leave.

items.q: Is Relevant Search Media an SEO agency in the USA or in India?
items.a:
Both, honestly. The company is registered in New Delhi, India, and the whole team works US hours.

settings.title: Why is my SEO not working?

settings.editor: When an owner asks “why is my SEO not working?”, the answer is nearly always one of three failed checks. Every engine takes a person’s question and names the most relevant business it can trust, and it decides with the same three checks.
Those checks are the D’Souza Equation: Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose. That is why one fix works on Google, on Maps and in an AI answer.

settings.text: Read the equation in full

settings.title: Read fails: you cannot be found.
settings.text: The engine cannot tell plainly what the business is, where it works and what it answers. Nothing else counts until this passes.

settings.title: Confirm fails: AI names someone else.
settings.text: Your own site says it, but listings, reviews and mentions elsewhere do not say the same thing. The engine will not vouch for you.

settings.title: Choose fails: found, then passed over.
settings.text: People see you and then click, call or book someone else. Engines watch that choice and move the chosen business up.

settings.title: What should I check before I pay anyone to fix SEO problems?

settings.editor: Five checks, about ten minutes, no tools to buy. They tell you which problem you have, and they make any quote easier to judge.

settings.title: Search yourself
settings.text: Private window, your trade plus your city. Note whether you are on page one, on the map, or neither.

settings.title: Read your listing as a stranger
settings.text: Photos, hours, services, reviews and replies. Would you call this business?

settings.title: Ask an AI assistant
settings.text: Type the question a customer would ask. See which business it names, and why.

settings.title: Date the drop
settings.text: If calls fell, find the week it began. A date turns a mystery into a cause.

items.q: Why has my website traffic dropped overnight?
items.a:
An overnight fall across the whole site is usually technical: a noindex tag left on after a rebuild, a robots block, an expired certificate or a host problem.

If only search visits fell and the site works, look for a Google update or a change to your Business Profile on that date.

items.q: I lost rankings after an update. Will they come back?
items.a:
Sometimes, and nobody can promise it. Google re-weighs what it values at each update, so pages can return when they improve or when the next update lands.

If you lost rankings after an update, compare your pages with the ones that rose and close the gap.

items.q: Can a website redesign cause a traffic drop?
items.a:
Yes, and it is one of the most common causes. A redesign often changes page addresses, removes text Google relied on, or goes live with a noindex tag still in place.

Keep the old addresses or redirect each one, and check indexing the day the new site launches.

items.q: How do I know if Google penalised my site?
items.a:
Open Search Console and look at the Manual actions report. If Google has taken action, it says so there and names the reason.

Most falls are not penalties. They are updates, technical mistakes or stronger rivals, and each is handled differently.

items.q: Should I pay for ads until my traffic recovers?
items.a:
Ads can replace lost calls while the cause is fixed, and for some businesses that is the right bridge. They do not repair what caused the fall.

Find and fix the cause first, or the ads become a permanent cost for a problem that had a cure.

settings.title: The D'Souza Equation: Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose

settings.editor: The D'Souza Equation says Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose. A search engine or an AI assistant names a business when it can read plainly what the business is, when independent sources confirm it, and when real people choose it. The three are multiplied, so a business that fails one check is not named.
One equation. Every engine obeys it.

Ask a question

settings.editor: 20 to 30 minutes with Thomas. No audit to buy first.

• 900+ businesses served
  • 100+ specialists on US hours
  • In digital marketing since 2010

It is a way of seeing what every engine has to decide before it names a business. Google, Maps, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity look different, but each takes a person’s question and names the most relevant business it can trust.
Move the three dials below. The lights are customers asking, and the number is how many of every hundred are sent to you.

settings.plain: Out of 100 people who ask, the engine sends roughly {n} your way. Let one check fall to nothing and it sends none.

terms.name: Read
terms.q: Is it plain from the site itself who this is and which questions it settles?
terms.where: clear facts, direct answers, clean structure and markup on your own pages.

terms.name: Confirm
terms.q: Does the rest of the web describe the business the same way?
terms.where: matching listings, real reviews, mentions and press on other sites.

terms.name: Choose
terms.q: When shown this business, do searchers pick it?
terms.where: a listing and a first screen that win the click, the call and the return visit.

settings.editor: For example, when a customer asks “who fixes a burst pipe?”, the engine reads each plumber’s site, checks what others say, and looks at who people chose. With Read at 80, Confirm at 70 and Choose at 75, about 42 in 100 are sent to you.

settings.title: How do search engines rank websites?

settings.editor: How do search engines rank websites, and how do AI assistants pick one business to name? With three checks. Each check is a question the engine asks, and each has a place where the work is done.

settings.title: Read
settings.text: The engine has to understand the business from its own pages: who it is, what it does, where, and which questions it settles.

settings.title: Confirm

Evolving, in one direction: from ranking a page to being named as the answer. The reading has become stricter and the room at the top smaller.

A method built on the customer’s question absorbs each new engine as one more reader, without starting again.

settings.editor: How does Google search work? In three stages that Google itself names: it crawls the web to find pages, indexes what it understands of them, and serves the results it judges most useful for each search. settings.text: On page SEO: can every engine read you?

settings.caption: The three stages of Google search and what goes wrong at each

rows.b: Programs called crawlers follow links and fetch pages
rows.c: The page is blocked, unlinked or too slow to fetch

settings.editor: How do AI Overviews work? Google’s Gemini models read pages from Google’s own index and write a short summary above the results, with links to the pages they drew on. AI Mode does the same in a longer, conversational form.
They do not replace the three stages. They sit on top of them, so a page that was never crawled or indexed cannot be quoted in the summary.

settings.editor: How does ChatGPT search work? When a question needs current information, ChatGPT searches the web, reads a handful of pages and writes an answer that cites them. It also has its own crawler, OAI-SearchBot, which sites can allow or block by name.
Other assistants follow the same pattern with different sources. The reading is new; the need to be readable, confirmed and chosen is not.

settings.title: What do all of these have in common?

settings.editor: Each of them takes a person’s question and names the most relevant answer it can trust. That is the first observation behind the D’Souza Equation: Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose.
Crawling and indexing are Read. Agreement from other sources is Confirm. What people click, call and return to is Choose.

items.q: How Google search works, in one sentence?
items.a:
It finds pages, works out what each one is about, and for every search shows the pages it judges most useful to that person, in that place, at that moment.

Everything else, from links to reviews to AI summaries, is detail inside those three steps.

items.q: How does Google search work so fast?
items.a:
Because the hard work is done before you search. Google has already crawled and indexed the pages, so a search is a lookup in a prepared index, not a fresh read of the web.

That is also why a new page cannot appear until Google has crawled it.

items.q: How does the Google search engine work for a local search?
items.a:
For a local search Google adds place to the picture. It says local results turn mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, and it draws on Business Profiles as well as websites.

That is why a complete, accurate profile matters as much as the site.

items.q: Does Google search work the same for everyone?
items.a:
No. Results change with where you are, what you searched before and the device in your hand. Two people can type the same words and see different businesses.

A private window, on a phone, inside your service area gives the fairest test.

items.q: Does an AI answer use the same pages as search?
items.a:
Largely, yes. Google’s AI answers are written from pages in Google’s index, and assistants such as ChatGPT search the web and cite what they read.

A page that search engines cannot read is not available to quote in an AI answer either.
